headline: Four ancient populations
body: Same species, same biology, measurably different bones.
punch: And the biggest lever on height in history wasn't genetic.

headline: Researchers compared
body: Late Stone Age, Sadlermiut, Indian Knoll and Point Hope. They measured femur and humerus cortical thickness and shaft length across the populations.
punch: Skeletal growth compared at population scale.

headline: The differences
body: Not measurement noise. Real variation in how long bones got and how thick their walls became, between groups of the same species.
punch: Different growth outcomes from an identical template.

headline: The explanation
body: Population level differences in nutrition, mechanical loading and disease burden accounted for the variation better than ancestry did.
punch: Environment wrote more of the outcome than inheritance.

headline: The same thing happened
body: Populations gained substantial adult height across a few generations with no genetic change at all. The Dutch went from among Europe's shorter populations to its tallest inside a century.

headline: Which tells you
body: Nutritional adequacy, disease burden and mechanical loading during growth moved height by more than any pharmacology in this topic has ever demonstrated.
punch: The unglamorous inputs have the biggest effect sizes.

headline: And it explains
body: This is why a magnesium or protein shortfall damages growth plate architecture while supplementing above adequacy does nothing. You're either below the line or you aren't.
punch: Fixing a deficit is the whole mechanism.

headline: The honest limit
body: Diet and activity are inferred from skeletal remains rather than measured directly, and population averages don't predict any single person.
punch: Strong at population scale, silent about individuals.

headline: It's never over
body: Real mechanisms, real citations, no protocols.
